title: Leaders Can Carry Too Much Truth Through Humor
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article examines how leaders use humor as a socially safe vehicle for delivering criticism they'd rather not state directly. It explains humor's function as a form of plausible deniability, allowing leaders to say what they really think while retaining the ability to claim they were "only kidding." The piece warns that leaders who overuse this device create a defensive, on-edge climate where team members brace for the next "zinger," and closes by noting that jokes, in the workplace context, are a genuinely serious matter.
points: Leaders often use humor as a socially safe way to deliver criticism they'd otherwise avoid stating directly.
Humor functions as plausible deniability, letting leaders retreat to "I was only kidding" if a joke lands badly.
Overusing humor to convey criticism produces a defensive climate where team members brace for the next jab.
Team members may model this behavior themselves, pushing genuine criticism further underground.
Occasional, well-placed humor is fine, but it should not become a leader's primary vehicle for expressing dislikes.
quotes: There is a nugget of truth inside every joke or attempt at humor, at least in the mind of the teller.
Humor is a back door, an escape hatch, a source of plausible deniability, a way to insult without being caught red-handed.
They can always tell others they “were only kidding” to escape their obvious guilt.
While there is nothing wrong with an occasional tease or attempt at humor to carry a critical message, leaders who overuse this style often make others paranoid as they wait for the next “zinger.
As any comedian will tell you, a joke is a deadly serious thing.
